- **[X8-lib]** The provisional library manual of the *X8* system, section 7

- **[course]** E. W. Dijkstra, *Cursus programmeren in ALGOL 60*,

"Property n" is the n-th special property of [KA03, 1.3]; "stop n" is a

## The manual's rules are not the compiler's checks

The first version of this dialect refused programs that broke the
manual's rules. That was a misreading. [KA03, 1.3]: "The greatest
shortcoming of the system, however, was the almost complete absence of
syntax checks"; the only grammatical check was for undeclared identifiers.
And programs that break the rules compile with the real compiler: in
sergev's examples, `beer`, `disarium`, `magic_square`, `mersenne` and
`whetstone` declare procedures before variables (property 15), `lisp` and
`pentomino` put `if` after `do` (property 12), and `bulls_and_cows` has
`then if`, which even the Report forbids.

So `--x1` accepts such programs, with a warning naming the property: the
manual forbade it, the compiler did not check, and what followed is not
known. The run-time stops of appendix A (integer capacity, an array with a
lower bound above its upper) remain errors, since they really did stop the
X1.

| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| The step of `for V := A step B until C` | Evaluated twice each time round, after `V := A` | Once each time round, and the first time *before* `V := A` | Property 11; FOR1, FOR5–FOR7 in [KA-X1X8, 3.3.3] | `property_11_*` |
| `go to` an undefined switch designator | A dummy statement (4.3.5) | Undefined; here an error | Property 10 | `property_10_*` |
| `abs` | Real | The type of its argument | Property 6 | `property_6_*` |
| `sqrt`, `ln` of a negative number | Undefined | Of its absolute value | Property 6; [X1-man] point 6 | `property_6_*` |
| The value of a typed procedure | Converted to the declared type | "Determined by the arithmetic carried out this time" | Property 18 | `property_18_*` |
| Order of evaluating parameters called by value | Not fixed; left to right here | The order of the specifications | Property 22 | `property_22_*` |

`--x1` rounds it away from zero (Rust's `round`).

magnitude lies between 2⁻²⁰⁴⁸ (about .3094⏨−616) and about .1616⏨+617; on

least real, a number below it for the stack's zero, and the greatest f64

exponent would exceed 600, which is all three, is printed as "the integer

printed a mass of 0 as `+                  0` [Tract8, p. 106]. A result
smaller in magnitude than the stack's zero (such as `0 / 2`) is kept at
it, which is assumed. Values between 10³⁰⁸ and 10⁶¹⁶, or
between 10⁻³⁰⁸ and 10⁻⁶¹⁶, are not modelled.

the least real is about 1.49⏨−154 here, where the X1's would be 2⁻¹⁰²⁴,

stand-in's, not the X1's. TPK meets this when an input is 0: `sqrt(abs(t))`

number is evidence only that the result was not 0.

## The manual's rules (warnings)

| Property | Warned about |
| --- | --- |
| 5 | A standard function (`abs` ... `entier`) called as a statement |
| 12 | A conditional statement straight after `do` |
| 13 | A parameter delimiter other than a comma, such as `) Order: (` |
| 15 | Declarations other than in the order scalars, arrays, switches, procedures; specifications other than scalars and strings, arrays, labels and switches, procedures |
| 17 | Bounds that are not integer numbers, for an `own` array or one in the outermost block |
| 19 | A formal parameter without a specification |
| 21 | A label in the value list |
| [KA03, ch. 7] | `abs`, `sign`, `sqrt`, `sin`, `cos`, `ln`, `exp`, `entier`, `read`, `print`, `TAB`, `NLCR`, `SPACE` as actual parameters: operators of the run-time complex, not procedures. [sergev] documents the compiler producing bad code for some of these |

Property 8, labels that begin with a digit, is an error: the real
compiler stops with a fatal error on `10:` (`compare/probes/numeric-label.a60`).
So is property 1, a labelled program: Knuth and Trabb Pardo's TPK begins
`TPK: begin`, and the real compiler stops with 0–25, "exhausted source
store" (`compare/probes/tpk-1976.a60`).
Property 23 (a value array has at most five subscripts) is an error at the
call. Not checked: properties 2, 9, 16 and 20.

A value part after a specification (`real t; value t;`, as in TPK) is
not among the manual's properties. The Report forbids it (5.4.1), and so
does the Report dialect here. The X1 compiler accepted it but compiled t
as a value array (`compare/probes/value-after-spec.a60`), so `--x1` warns,
and calls t by value. (Knuth's errata for the 2003 reprint of the paper
correct the heading to the Report's order, 12 February 2014.)

## The library

`read`, `print`, `TAB`, `NLCR`, `SPACE`, `stop`, `SUM`, `PRINTTEXT`, `FLOT`,
`FIXT`, `ABSFIXT` and `EVEN` (the prefill of the name list in x1algol.pas),
with the meanings of [course], [MR54] and [X8-lib], checked against the
X1's own output [Tract8]:

- `print(x)`: by the type of x [course; MR54]. An integer "in at most
  eight decimals, non-significant zeros replaced by spaces", with its
  sign: `FIXT(8, 0, x)`. A real by `FLOT(13, 3, x)`, "the fraction in the
  computing precision" (13 digits is the X8's), or as 0 or `inf` beyond an
  exponent of 600. Then the start of the next column; "at most 7 columns
  are typed on a line" [course]. The X1's column width is not known; the
  X8's 21 positions are kept.
- `ABSFIXT(n, m, x)`: a space, |x| with n digits before the point and m
  after, leading zeros as spaces (the units zero too, unless m = 0), a
  space. `FIXT` puts the sign in place of the first space: "Typt teken,
  n decimale cijfers van geheel deel van x, ..." [MR54], and the X1
  printed `+ 3.429474152`, `- .049534455` [Tract8]. (The X8 manual puts
  the sign beside the first digit; this dialect did so until the X1's
  output was found.)
- `FLOT`: sign, point, mantissa between .1 and 1, ⏨, signed exponent. The
  X8's has three parameters (n, m, x). **The X1's has two**: Zonneveld's
  program calls `FLOT(12, x)`. Its exponent has two digits: "the number
  of decimals for the exponent was here fixed to two" [KA-X1X8, appendix
  A, note 3]. x1sim's `FLOT` has the same layout.
- `TAB` to the next multiple of 8 (at least 2 on), `SPACE(n)`, `NLCR`; a
  line of 144 positions, beyond which a new line is begun.
- `SUM(i, a, b, x)` and `EVEN(n)` as the manual declares them.

`XEEN`, which reads the operator's console, is not provided. The
procedures of the Modified Report (`outstring`, `outreal` ...) are kept so
that the same test programs run in both dialects; the X1 did not have
them.

## Compared with the real compiler on sergev's simulator

`compare/` runs 33 probe programs through `--x1` and through the real 1964
compiler on x1sim; [`compare/README.md`](../compare/README.md) has the
table, and says which results are decided by the compiler (and so are
evidence about the X1) and which by the run-time (two reconstructions).
In brief:

- **Confirmed by the real compiler**: value parameters evaluated in the
  order of specification (property 22), nine symbols of an identifier
  (property 3), `then if` with `else` on the nearest `if`, both operands
  of `∧` and `∨` evaluated, and programs that break the manual's rules
  compiling (properties 15 and 19; Knuth's program as printed gives −67).
- **Confirmed for the order of evaluation**: primaries left to right
  (property 7), a variable fetched before a later function call in the
  same expression changes it, subscripts left to right, and in an

- **Where the X1 user manual [X1-man] decides against x1sim**: a real

## 7. Library procedures

The provisional library of the ALGOL system for the X8 contains
the following groups of procedures, which do not need to be
declared in the program:

### 7.1. Elementary functions

### 7.2. Input procedures

As input device a tape reader is available, with a speed of
1000 punches/second for 5-, 7-, or 8-hole punched tape. There
are three input procedures for the tape reader:

**7.2.3.** `real procedure READ;`

The function designator READ has meaning only if the input tape
is punched according to the punching conventions for number
tapes, shown in 8. The value of READ is the value of the next
number on the tape, with a relative precision of approximately
12 decimal places, in absolute value between the limits 10^-616
and 10^628 or exactly 0. Integers on the tape, in absolute
value smaller than 1 099 511 627 776, are entered exactly.

The relation <number> = READ is true if the decimal
representation of <number> in the ALGOL text and of the number
found by READ on the number tape are the same.

**7.2.4.** `real procedure read; read:= READ;`

`read` is just another name for READ.

### 7.3. Output procedures

For the time being, the following output devices are available:

  * a line printer, with a speed of 7 to 20 lines/second. Per page, 60 lines with a width of 144 positions are available,
  * a tape punch for 7-hole tape with a speed of 150 heptades/second.

The use of the tape punch as an output device is only recommended for outputting data that

  * must be read in again later,
  * must be published in a nicer typography than that of the line printer,
  * must be mechanically multiplied.

If you only have a few final answers, but also want to output
many intermediate results in order to be able to check them in
case of doubt, you can:

  * output the intermediate results on the line printer,
  * punch the final answers.

**7.3.1.2.** `procedure SPACE (n); value n; integer n;`

SPACE basically increases the position on the line by n. If the
number of symbols on the line threatens to exceed 144, the
system inserts as many line advances (each time decreasing the
position on the line by 144) as necessary to guarantee the
correct line width. SPACE (n) is equivalent to, but faster
than:

    begin integer i; for i := 1 step 1 until n do PRSYM (93) end;

**7.3.1.3.** `procedure TAB;`

TAB in principle increases the position on the line by at least
2 and at most 9, so that an 8-fold is achieved (the positions
on the line are numbered from 0 to 143. The "tab stops" are
therefore located at the positions numbered 8, 16, 24, ... 136).
If the line width is exceeded, a line advance is inserted
and the position on the line is reduced by 144.

**7.3.1.4.** `procedure NLCR;`

NLCR provides a line feed and resets the position on the line
to 0. If executing NLCR would cause the number of lines on the
page to exceed 60, a transition to a new page is accomplished
instead of a line feed.

import re, sys

            "true", "false", "goto", "own", "switch", "string", "label"]

IDIOM_OLD = "the input and output procedures ininteger, outinteger and outstring as the interpreter gives them (IFIP 1964, systems file)"
IDIOM_NEW = ("the X1 system's input and output procedures read, print, PRINTTEXT and NLCR, as the harness README "
             "gives them (harnesses/algol-60/README.md, 2.1) and its own X1 programs cite them (Kruseman Aretz 2003, "
             "chapter 7), and the X1 compiler's representation, with underlined reserved words and the operator "
             "symbols (harness README, 2.1)")

    return "".join(c + "̲" for c in w.lower())


def balanced(s, i):
    """s[i] == '(' ; return index after the matching ')'."""
    depth = 0
    j = i
    while True:
        c = s[j]
        if c == '"':
            j = s.index('"', j + 1)
        elif c == "(":
            depth += 1
        elif c == ")":
            depth -= 1
            if depth == 0:
                return j + 1
        j += 1


def io_call(name, args):
    if name == "ininteger":
        a, v = args.split(",", 1)
        assert a.strip() == "0", args
        return [v.strip() + " := read"]
    if name == "outinteger":
        a, e = args.split(",", 1)
        assert a.strip() == "1", args
        return ["print(" + e.strip() + ")"]
    a, t = args.split(",", 1)
    assert a.strip() == "1", args
    t = t.strip()
    assert t[0] == '"' and t[-1] == '"', t
    t = t[1:-1]
    out = []
    parts = t.split("\\n")
    for k, p in enumerate(parts):
        assert "\\" not in p, p
        bad = set(p) - ALLOWED
        assert not bad, (p, bad)
        if p:
            out.append("PRINTTEXT(`" + p + "')")
        if k < len(parts) - 1:
            out.append("NLCR")
    return out

    out = []
    i = 0
    n = len(src)

### P04: each relation a procedure that passes on its solutions

ALGOL 60 has no unknowns and no alternatives. Each relation is transcribed as
a procedure with one branch per case, in the order written, that passes each
of its solutions to a parameterless procedure `found` and returns when it has
no more; a disjunction calls its alternatives one after the other, in the
order written. An unknown is a Boolean that says whether it has a value and a
variable that holds it, both passed by name; a value given to an unknown is
taken back when `found` returns. The continuation `found` is often a procedure
declared in an inner block of the caller, which is the way Knuth's man or boy
test passes its procedure `B` (1964; `examples/man-or-boy-1964.alg` in the
image). Sequences are batch 1A's cells; the atom ᴀ is the code 1.

- **P04a, P04b.** `loop(x)` is its one case, a procedure that calls itself.
  P04a calls `loop` and then `x = k`; P04b the other way round. In P04a `loop`
  never returns, so `x = k` is never reached; in P04b `x = k` is reported
  first. Neither finishes: in report and x1 the expectation is the budget, in
  x1sim (no budget) the safety limit or the X1's stack.
- **P04c, P04d (alist-left).** Case 1 is tried first, with its conjuncts in the
  order written: `alist(m)` is called with m unknown, and only then is
  `s = ⟨ᴀ⟩ ++ m` decided (`conseq`, which gives m from s, or s from m, or
  tests it). So the recursion on case 1 comes first, at every depth, whether s
  is known (P04c) or not (P04d). No reordering was made to avoid it: it is the
  presentation order the problem fixes.
- **P04e, P04f (alist-right).** Case 1, s = ⟨⟩, first; then case 2. With s
  known (P04e) the head of case 2 gives m from s, and then `alist(m)` is
  called. With s unknown (P04f) the head cannot give s a value before m has
  one (there are no partial values), so `alist(m)` is called first and the
  head then gives s: **one move** (rule 4), in both texts, since both contain
  the procedure. The test of whether s is known, which chooses between the two
  orders, is R. P04f prints ⟨⟩, ⟨ᴀ⟩, ⟨ᴀ,ᴀ⟩, … until it is stopped; the harness
  collects the first 20.
- Counters `[operations alist/1 N]`, `alist/2`, `loop/1` (H) count a case when
  it is taken. A stage that never ends prints no observe block.
- R, by the author's reading: the known-flags and the parameter `found` (extra
  arguments, rule 5), the taking back of a value after `found` returns, the
  test of which places are known, and P04f's move. Giving back the cell made
  for a value (`top := top - 1`) only lets store be reused: C (rule 16).

### P05: the values of x held all at once

`pick(x)` is its facts, read from the constants: when it is posed each fact,
in order, gives x one value, and the values are held all at once, each with a
Boolean that says whether it is still a solution. Each comparison or equation
is held as posed until x has values, and is then tested on each value
(testing a fully known relation is P); a value that fails is dropped and not
kept. Before `pick` (P05b, stage 1), the comparison is held, and the answer is
`x held, where x gt 1`. Each stage prints one answer per value still held, or
none and `no solution` in the observe block. The observe block lists the values
held, `[problem-alternatives x N]` (the problem-defined alternatives,
`METRICS.md`), the held relations with `[suspended held-relations N]` while one
waits, and `[operations pick/i 1]` for each fact applied. It does not print
`[alternatives …]`, since nothing is left for a request for more answers to
resume: every value held is printed (ambiguity 7). Comparisons are printed in
words (`x gt 1`, `not (x = 2)`), since the X1 code has no `>` in strings.

### P06: negation

- **P06a, P06c, P06b.** As P01 and P02 in batch 1A: x is a Boolean and an
  integer; `not (x = c)` is held while x is unknown, and is tested with the
  negation of the language, `¬(x = c)`, once x is known; `x = c` gives x its
  value or is tested. The answer before x is known is
  `x held, where not (x = 1)`. P06c's stage 2 makes the held negation false,
  and the program reports no answer and `no solution`.
- **P06d.** `mem` is a Boolean procedure testing mem(e, s) with both known, its
  cases in order: case 1 when the head is e, else case 2 on the tail (once
  case 1 has made it true, case 2 is not tried: a test needs one derivation).
  `setdiff` computes d from s1 and s2 as a function, the direction the query
  uses, by its three cases in order, case 3 testing its own conjunct
  `¬mem(h, s2)` (so mem is evaluated again there). Mode-faithful (rule 3):
  *expressible*.
- **P06e1, P06e2, P06e3.** The facts of the closed world are arrays read from
  the constants, atoms as codes (ʙʀᴏᴡɴ 1, ꜱᴍɪᴛʜ 2, ᴄ101 101, ᴄ301 301).
  `nonmajor` is its one case, its conjuncts in order: `student(p)` is tested
  on each fact (p known, P06e1 and P06e2) or gives p each fact's value (P06e3),
  `maths(k)` gives k each fact's value, and `takes(p, k)`, both known, is a
  Boolean procedure over its facts, negated with `¬`. So p and k are always
  known when the negation is decided, as the observe block says. Each
  derivation is one answer (`true`, or `p = brown`). Each program uses one
  direction only: *expressible*.

### P07: one relation at a time

Batch 1A's design for P02: each relation held as posed, its evaluator
giving the remaining place its value when enough are known or testing it,
and a loop examining the held relations in the order posed until a pass gives
no unknown a value. x + y + z = 12 has one evaluator for the three-place sum
(writing it compound or decomposed is a transcription, `SPECIFICATION.md`).

- **P07a** solves z, then y, then x, in every order; the order changes only
  the number of passes, which the counters `[operations R1-examined N]` show.
- **P07b, P07c, P07f** have no relation with a known place, so nothing is
  given a value: the relations are held and reported as such
  (`x held, y held, where x + y = 10, x - y = 4`). P07f's inconsistency is
  not detected. Solving P07b by elimination would be an algorithm the problem
  does not state (and, written generally, a solver over relations, S); it was
  not written (ambiguity 9).
- **P07d, P07e.** w · u = v, as P02's R2: w from v and u where u divides v,
  `no solution` where it does not (P07e: 15 is not a multiple of 2).
- **P07g.** x · x = c has one unknown in both its factors, and c known, so its
  evaluator gives x its values: r = entier(sqrt(c) + 0.5) and, if r · r = c,
  r and −r (one value if r = 0), and none if c is negative or not a square.
  Two answers, `x = 3` and `x = -3`, and the values held all at once in the
  observe block. That this is computing a place of the relation (P, rule 19)
  and not a changed algorithm is the author's reading (ambiguity 10).

### P08: a definition that arrives

ALGOL 60 has no definitions that arrive while a program runs: every procedure
is in the text before the program starts. So the procedures `rev` and `conc`
(transcribed as in batch 1A's P03, each computing its last place by its cases
in order) are in the text, and a Boolean for each definition, or each case,
says whether it has arrived. The stage that brings a definition sets it. An
application of `rev` before its definition has arrived is held as posed,
neither true nor false, and examined again at each later stage: **the fourth
of the problem's four states, a computation awaiting its definition**, which is
the open reading. The observe block says which definitions have arrived, shows
the application as `rev((x, y, z), b) awaiting its definition`, and gives
`[suspended pending-applications 1]` while it is held.

- **P08a, P08b.** The elements of a sequence are indices into a table of
  elements, each a Boolean and an integer: 1 is x, 2 is y, 3 is z, and the
  elements of stage 6's sequence are further entries with their values.
  `rev` and `conc` only move elements, so they work on elements with no value:
  at stage 4, b = (z, y, x). x = y and y = z are held until one side is known,
  as P01a's equations. b = s ++ c, with b known, equates each element of s
  with the element of b in its place, which gives z its value, and c is the
  rest of b; then y = z and x = y give y and x theirs. Answers name every
  unknown, as its value, `held` or `free`, with the relations held, for
  example after stage 4:
  `a = (x, y, z), b = (z, y, x), c free, x held, y held, z free, where x = y`.
  P08b stops after stage 3 with the application still held, which the
  observe block tells apart from failure.
- **P08c.** conc's definition arrives at stage 1, rev's case 1 at stage 3, as
  the two sequences of the stage's constants (ambiguity 2), and rev's case 2 at
  stage 4. `rev` and `conc` say whether they found their result (1), found
  there is none (0), or could not tell because a case they would need has not
  arrived (2). At stage 3, case 1 does not apply to ⟨1, 2⟩ and case 2 has not
  arrived, so the application is still held; at stage 4 it is decided,
  b = (2, 1). The application is held until the whole of rev and conc has
  arrived, even after a case that has arrived gives a solution.
- R, by the author's reading: the holding of the application and of the
  equations, the flags that say a definition has arrived, and the tests of
  them (ambiguity 3 asks whether those tests are C instead, by rule 11).
- Integers in P08's answers are printed by an output adapter, digit by digit,
  so that an answer with many values stays inside the X1 system's line of 144
  positions, where `print` takes a column of its own for each value; the
  report text does the same, for parity.

7. **P05: are the values held "alternatives pending"?** They are all printed

## ALGOL 60, batch 1B (P04–P08): summary

I committed the work as `37cdeda` on the branch `implementation-algol-60` in `~/cp-roles/implementation-1B-algol-60`. The author is `implementation-algol-60 <implementation-algol-60@sandbox>`, there are no trailers, and nothing is pushed. It holds 148 files: 26 programs in each of the three configurations, their constants files, and a new batch 1B section in `programs/algol-60/README.md`.

`check` reports no error and no warning for any of the 78 programs (26 in report, 26 in x1, 26 in x1sim). Nothing else was run on any program.

**Programs.** Every program is primary; no named variants were written. Each sub-problem has `report/<id>.alg` plus `x1/<id>.a60` and `x1sim/<id>.a60`:
- **P04a–f:** reposed. Each relation is a procedure, one branch per case, in the order written, that hands each solution to a parameterless procedure parameter. The presentation order is kept, so P04a, P04c and P04d will run until they are stopped. P04f has one move: the body comes before the head when s is unknown.
- **P05a–c:** incremental. pick's facts give x its values, all held at once; each comparison or equation waits until x has values, then is tested on each.
- **P06a, b, c:** incremental. The negation waits while x is unknown, then is tested with `¬`.
- **P06d:** setdiff and mem written as functions, one branch per case (case 3 tests `¬mem` itself).
- **P06e1–e3:** the closed-world facts are arrays; nonmajor is its one case, conjuncts in order.
- **P07a–g:** reposed. Batch 1A's approach: each relation waits until enough places are known. P07b, P07c and P07f stay unsolved and are reported as held relations; P07e's contradiction is detected. P07g uses sqrt to give x = 3 and x = −3.
- **P08a–c:** incremental. The application of rev is held, neither true nor false, until its definition has arrived (state 4, the open reading).

**Expressibility (my reading).** P06d and P06e1–e3 are *expressible*. Everything else is *expressible with reformulation*. Nothing was judged not expressible.

**Shared texts.**
- x1 and x1sim are byte-identical everywhere. The X1 texts were made from the report texts by a text-substitution script; I disclosed this in the README.
- Within each configuration: P06a = P06c, P06e1 = P06e2, P07d = P07e, and P08a = P08b (P08b has no constants file).
- One P07a program and one constants file serve all six P07a instances, because the constants do not depend on the order.

**Ambiguities, with the reading I took** (in full in the README):
1. P08 says rev and conc are "as in P03", but P03's file was not in my reading list. I took the definitions from batch 1A's P03 programs.
2. P08c stage 3 gives rev's case 1 with constants (`rev(<seq>, <seq>)`). The program reads them from the constants. If a variant made case 1 overlap case 2, only case 1's solution would be reported.
3. ALGOL 60 cannot receive a definition while the program runs. The definitions are in the text and a flag marks their arrival, and I judged that not to be anticipation. A classifier could instead call P08 not expressible, or class the flag tests as C (rule 11) rather than R.
4. In P08c, with only part of rev defined, the application is tried with the cases that have arrived and held until the whole definition is there.
5. P04's solution-passing procedures could be read as a depth-first search mechanism (S). That would make P04 not expressible as the configurations are listed, and these programs named variants.
6. P04 keeps the presentation order even where it means the program never finishes.
7. P05's values are reported as `[problem-alternatives x N]`, not `[alternatives …]`, because the harness would read the latter as "alternatives pending".
8. P06e reports one answer per derivation, so duplicates are possible.
9. P07b and P07f are not solved by elimination.
10. I read P07g's square root as computing a place of the relation (P), not a changed algorithm.
11. Unknowns hold only integers; atoms are integer codes.
